fixes.explanation: Joash listens. The officials of Judah come and pay homage, and the verse says, “…and he listened to them.” Friend, I can be talked into anything by one person who says my cookies look nice, so I won't pretend I'd have done better.

Wrath is the word. Verse 18 says, “So wrath came upon Judah and Jerusalem for this guilt of theirs.” Just before that, the verse says they abandoned the house of the LORD and served the Asherah poles and idols. That's a strong word, baker, and the text uses it plainly.
Drought isn't in this verse. The text says, “So wrath came upon Judah and Jerusalem for this guilt of theirs.” The word it names is wrath.

Listen is the word. Verse 19 says the LORD sent prophets “…to bring the people back to Him and to testify against them, but they would not listen.” The prophets came to bring them back, and the people would not listen. I think it stings when you say something and nobody looks up.

Fight isn't the word here. The verse says the LORD sent prophets “…to bring the people back to Him and to testify against them, but they would not listen.” The word the text gives is listen. A person can ignore a message without raising a hand, and we all know somebody who's done it.

Worshiping isn't what God names. Through Zechariah, son of Jehoiada the priest, He asks, “Why do you transgress the commandments of the LORD so that you cannot prosper?” (2 Chronicles 24:20). He asks why, and in the same breath He names what it costs them. That cost is prospering, friend.

Resting isn't in the question. Zechariah, son of Jehoiada the priest, says, “Why do you transgress the commandments of the LORD so that you cannot prosper?” (2 Chronicles 24:20). The text says prosper, and it doesn't mention rest at all.

That's not what the text says. Through Zechariah, God says, “Because you have forsaken the LORD, He has forsaken you.” Those are the words in verse 20, baker. The people forsook the LORD, and the message says He has forsaken them.

False is right. The verse says, “But they conspired against Zechariah, and by order of the king, they stoned him in the courtyard of the house of the LORD.” The order came from King Joash. It's a heavy part of the story, friend.

The text doesn't say courage. Verse 22 says Joash “…failed to remember the kindness that Zechariah’s father Jehoiada had extended to him.” Kindness is what Jehoiada showed, and Joash forgot it. Instead, the verse says, Joash killed Jehoiada's son. It's a heavy verse, friend.

Those are his words. As Zechariah lay dying, he said, “May the LORD see this and call you to account.” (2 Chronicles 24:22). He asks the LORD to see what happened, and he asks for a calling to account. I think this one hurts, friend.

That isn't what Zechariah says. As he lay dying, he said, “May the LORD see this and call you to account.” (2 Chronicles 24:22). He asks the LORD to see what happened, and forgiveness isn't in his words. I think this is a heavy moment, and the text records his words just as they are.

His words in this verse don't mention his father's house. Zechariah, as he lay dying, said, “May the LORD see this and call you to account.” (2 Chronicles 24:22). I think it's a hard verse to sit with, so take your time on it, baker.

True. Verse 23 says the army of Aram “…entered Judah and Jerusalem and destroyed all the leaders of the people…” They also sent all the plunder to their king in Damascus. That's a heavy sentence, and it means what it says.

Verse 24 says, “Although the Aramean army had come with only a few men, the LORD delivered into their hand a very great army.” Few men, a very great army, and the verse says the LORD is the one who delivered it. It also gives the reason: “Because Judah had forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers, judgment was executed on Joash.”

Sleeping isn't mentioned in this verse. The text says, “Although the Aramean army had come with only a few men, the LORD delivered into their hand a very great army.” The verse says the LORD delivered it. That's how the text explains it, baker.
The text doesn't say sons. It says, “His own servants conspired against him…” Servants is the word the verse gives, and that's the one to hold on to.

False is right. Verse 25 says he “…was buried in the City of David, but not in the tombs of the kings.” So he's buried in the City of David, just not in the tombs of the kings. It's a small detail, friend, and it says a lot.
